It isn't perfect. There are some inconsistencies here and there, along with the UI being somewhat unwieldy. That being said, this is probably one of the better mecha games I've played in awhile. I would recommend it as a "soft yes", which will most likely become a "hard, erect, yes" after some polishing and updates. EDIT: The dev seems VERY active. Already pushing two-three hot-fixes right out the gate. +2

Its a clunky mech game with lots of clunky controls and a clunky interface. The balance between gathering upgrades and repair parts for your mech is twitchy at best. Enemies spawning very close out of nowhere can get a bit old. Its not *bad* but it definitely needs polishing before I'd put a "Good" sticker on it.

So, after emptying my missile pod and massive shoulder cannon into this enemy fortress... I am Literally rollerblading into melee behind a raised shield and krumping foes with a huge pilebunker arm while my buddy rains gatling fire and missiles from above like a disgustingly fat homesick veritech. This is pretty damn Kino. It's also hilarious when said friend runs out of bullets/missiles and is reduced to shin-kicking enemies as you spectate after your glorious death to a mind boggling swarm of enemies. All that remained was to pick up and deliver "the package" (i.e. BOMB) and deliver it. But gatling arms do not make for good manual dexterity. And as I said, all he could do was kick the foes in their shins. He died, and we both failed the resistance on the very cusp of victory. But many chuckles, lulz, and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥'s were had, and that was just our very first multiplayer session. Game is good fun.

这sb时间机制不改不值得好评。改机甲花时间，开个市场耗时间，买弹药耗时间。去年还是前年的demo就吐槽过了，结果糟粕留到现在？ 举个例子，第三个情景的弹药是工厂生产的，得下个任务才能造出来，既然是工厂生产的，不是军火商购买运过来的，为啥还要耗费我两个小时，我一个驾驶员还得帮你搬材料还是咋的？外头玩命打千禧，回头造个弹药还要拿我当黑奴是吧？而且你下个任务才能造好弹药那我这个任务怎么办？疯狂按F把对面踢死吗？ 既然说到时间那咱们就好好捋捋：修部件，搜废品，报废装备每次耗时间没问题。你改机甲时间一次性，去市场第一次扣时间我也懒得评价，为什么去了市场买每件东西都得额外花时间？bro去超市购物是买一瓶酱油，回家，然后再去超市再买瓶油再送回家吗？你改成每次购物可以选择多加钱，就当是多招点走私避开公司监管不就行了，非得惦记你那b时间是吧？

Look. I don't make the rules, but these are the facts: If you've ever posted some comment or thread like "Why don't they make more mecha games?" it's your ethical duty to buy this. Thankfully it's pretty fun, with just the right amount of rough edges that I like in games like this. Mechanics are simple, missions are quick, and it's got multiplayer.

Good potential. But not worth the money. I won`t refund this as i still have some hope. But only some. As of now, after a brief "wow" period you understand at last some things. -UI is plain bad. I saw worse, but that`s just awful. Mech and parts performance representation don`t really give needed information. -Game process is clunky, controls feels meh, but in fact they are way below that level. I`t s ok in MWO, when you pilot King crab. He is bulky and unresponsive. When all the game like this... no. Item management in mission... even Tetris on max speed feels better. Mob spawn, mob movements, mob evading and engaging is all... just wrong. Manageable. but wrong. For example game has melee. But all the idea is centered around not to get hit too much and spend a fortune on repairs,,, but in melee build you re bound to be hit. alot. Aaaand adding insult to injury, enemy mechs can and will blow up point-blank... -Game way too restrictive. I played more than one game like Darkest Dungeon, and i know how bad it can be. But it usually serves specific purpose in-game and have all corresponding mechanics so we can feel satisfaction by clever overcoming. But here we can clearly see dav pursuing hardcore for the sole reason of it. Like he watched some Dark Souls letsplay and said to himself "Ah! that`s the secret of blockbuster game! Difficulty! Player must not only struggle with inconvinient UI and controls. He must suffer RNG! He must suffer limitations! More obstacles for the Obstacle God!" No, sorry. It work for some guys who just like being frustrated. I don`t.

This review is a personal "NO" for myself. But I will address some issues for others that may want to know. The game is nothing like Mechwarrior And there is no meta progression. What this game is: Roguelike run until you die and start over. If you are looking for a game that has mechwarrior vibes.... This is not it. If you are looking for a Roguelike with a Bot you can customize with various campaigns - this is for you. The Game itself is not bad.. for what it is - but there are some things I personally do not like (No Traditional Radar). The Dev still has more content on the way as of this post - and from what I have seen of his replies, He looks very proactive and involved in the game.
Fun fact: Depending on your build, you will either play Armored Core or Mechwarrior

Don't let this game fool you, it's not a roguelite. That would imply there's a degree of metaprogression to this game, which there is not. (Beyond the unlocking of certain mech parts, that still will never show up during your runs anyway, thanks to their rarity level. And no, keeping two (or less on higher difficulties) mech parts from a previous run is not a form of metaprogression, when the best choice is always to pick the damn cargo bay module, thanks to how limited a baseline mech's inventory is.) The game has such promise, but I've found it difficult to play beyond normal difficulty. There's just a number of things about the game that would need tweaking for me to enjoy it. Below are a list of things that are a matter of taste more than anything, but this game has so far left more of a bad taste in my mouth than a good one. - Weapon Accuracy: Weapons are rediculously innacurate. - Enemy Density: You're in a battlemech, known as a Granvir, which stands out above all other battlemechs save for the final bosses of each campaign. What this means is that the game is prone to throwing 20+ mechs at you even while solo. To compensate, enemy mechs are made of paper. - Visibility: Your mech does not have scanners, allowing you to catch enemy signatures from a distance, and your pilot has myopia. Your enemies do not have these issues and will move toward your location no matter where you are. Expect enemies to constantly sneak up on you, especially while looting. - Noise: Because enemy mechs make the same noise as your mech, your own noise will make enemy mechs sneak up on you easier. - Elite Hunters: So, if you kill enough mechs during a campaign over a short period, you will trigger elite hunters. This is just a squad of 3-6 mechs that are a ltitle tougher than the rest, but here's the issue. You get no advance warning whatsoever, and they spawn almost immediately in your face, usually when your pants are down and you are reloading your weapons from a previous combat that triggered them in the first place. Unless you're in a very fast mech (and fast mechs are the meta), you're facing unavoidable damage. - RNG: Especially on higher difficulties, you live and die by the diceroll of what parts you acquire during your missions. Even if you play well, there's no way to beat the boss from the first campaign without a good pair of high movement speed legs, since he'll just otherwise run up to you and repeatedly club you to death, and make all the effort you put into that campaign a total waste. Now luckily, Zero Front is a short campaign, lasting about 30 minutes to an hour, but still, waste of time. The others however are /signficantly longer/. Here's my suggestion if you feel the same, don't feel afraid to savescum. The game doesn't save your gamestate when you alt-F4 out of a mission and that allows you to retry it.

When I play mech games, my preferred loadout is to use swords (preferably energy), use NO GUNS and move REAL FAST. When I started the first campaign, I moved really slow and had a combat dagger, but then I got ROCKET SKATES and a RINGBLADE, which instead of stabbing things with I spun around in a circle like some sort of beyblade slasher. And then I got a SECOND RINGBLADE, so I just ZOOMED AROUND, CUTTING EVERYTHING TO PIECES, it was amazing.

Made a mech with 4 arms, a gun in each hand and 4 guns in 2 double holsters. It was too many guns to the point the menu went off screen and I couldn't reload them properly, but it still shredded enemies none the less. 11/10 would mildly inconvenience myself again.

[h3]机甲是一辈子的浪漫啊！[/h3] 说实话，机甲的诱惑，相信没有多少人能抵挡得住；当一个由齿轮零件等等成千上百个钢铁零件组装在一起的庞然巨物出现在你面前之时，它就是机械美学的极致与巅峰。 而当机甲与肉鸽战役的随机策略性相结合，便成就了《Granvir》这样一款以 “建造+战斗” 为核心的游戏。游戏中玩家操控 “Granvir” 机甲，在战火纷飞的土地上，用战场上搜刮的零件即时拼装机体、用武器去战斗厮杀、再用资源升级自己的机甲，如此形成一个正反馈循环。 游戏最亮眼的设计，自然便是将 “机甲拼装” 与 “实时战斗” 缝在了一起，实现了 “边打边升级” 的循环。可以说战场就是玩家的零件库，获得的腿部、手臂、特殊模块等等，捡起来就能直接换装到机甲上。这种多变快节奏的玩法，让每一场战斗都充满变数：可能前一秒还在用大剑近战劈砍，下一秒换上加农炮和火箭巢，就能切换成无限火力覆盖的自走炮台。这种 “没有固定套路，全凭战场捡装” 的玩法，可以说打破了很多游戏预设build的束缚，每一次出击都是全新的战斗体验。 本作的武器库为不同战斗风格的玩家提供了充足选择，近战与远程的混搭组合几乎没有限制。近战端有光束剑、火箭长矛、打桩机；远程端则有加农炮、机关枪、火焰喷射器等等，可以说十分丰富。同样的，玩家也可以自由选择自己的战术，可以当一个近战莽夫冲脸开莽，也可以做远程炮台猥琐输出。不同的组合策略，让每场战斗的每台 Granvir 都成为玩家独一无二的载具。 总而言之如果你渴望体验 “边打边拼、即时进化” 的新奇机甲战斗体验，那么《Granvir》绝对值得一试。 [quote]关注[url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/36224058/]老实人鉴赏家 [/url] [url=https://steamcommunity.com/groups/laoshirenLSR]老实人评测[/url]：独立游戏爱好者聚集地，黄油绅士交流中心。 不错过游戏的亮点，不放过游戏的槽点，带给玩家最直观的测评感受。[/quote]

[h3]这对我而言是一款很有趣的机甲题材游戏，当然，对其他人而言可能就只剩有趣了。[/h3] 首先要说一点就是汉化没有跟上英语的进度并且偏机翻（也可能是我没理解用意），许多英语更改的词汇汉语还没有更进。 偏美式机甲的笨重风格，几乎完全定制的模块化组装，要手臂要侧武器都行，而且近战流也确实能玩（应该可以这么说）。同类型的几乎都是联机游戏，其他的要么是日式机甲，要么点进去一看是战棋，要么就躲不掉强制联网的命运。虽然同题材的游戏我只有几个，但提供类似沙盒模式的我知道的就只有两款。 现有的剧情战役只有三个，而且在有昼夜变化的同时使用了偏愚蠢的时间管理系统。这游戏弹药也占用背包，虽然正常情况下说弹药是充足的，但总是会到需要多的弹药占用背包的时候。几乎完全是独自作战，你能遇到的仅有的队友通常伤害不高并且跟不上你的步伐。而且沙盒模式只提供你曾接触过的装备，想要解锁全部装备需要点手段，并且至少通过所有战役一遍（我是这么认为）。 总体评价其实是 [b]不推荐 [/b]，但我依然选择好评的形式发出来，对于喜欢这个题材的人我的评价是可以考虑入手，希望开发商能完善翻译并提供更多不同类型的战役。
很有意思的机甲游戏，机体和武器配件种类丰富，三个战役通关一遍后基本都能见得到。建议每种零件和武器都尝试一下，以找出最适合自己战斗风格的最佳组合。 游戏风格前期像是机甲战士，后期像是前线任务。 推荐喜欢机甲题材的玩家，虽然总体上机体偏笨重，但后期配件搭配也可以组装出异常灵活的机体。

[h1]The Mech-Building Game![/h1] Probably the best potential for the greatest mech game of all time, but it does have some glaring issues after having me and my team play it for a total of about 13 hours. This is a review for players looking for a challenge with a team or solo. I will be reviewing only the hard/hardest difficulty of the game. As "Normal" is targeted for a very casual audience, as Dev stated: "Hard was the original difficulty and is the one I tune for requiring you to engage with all the mechanics. Normal loosens the reigns and you can ignore a lot of stuff and still win." [h3]Mediocre replay value.[/h3] - You will notice that most if not all maps are fixed and very similar if not the same. - Builds usually all go towards one thing, which is speed, as Viper told me, "Speed is life" - [strike]In multiplayer, sometimes the party gets resistance support, which is the same 3-5 items for everyone, which butchers any diversity you had in your team. Got that T3 cool gun? Nice, now everyone builds around it![/strike] it is randomised now - Only a handful of pilots that have little to medium impact on your gameplay. [h3]Hardest Difficulty[/h3] Here it's kind of different for solo and multiplayer [b]Solo Experience.[/b] - On solo you're basically swarmed with tanky enemies, if you simply don't get a higher-tier (better than T1) weapon in the first 2-3 missions, the run is over. You can't really outskill enemies due to very limited early components. - Melee combat really boils down to damage trading. You can block with some weapons, which usually works well, but it's not viable for blocking any projectiles, and 60% of the time it won't save you from enemy melee mechs because they're usually backed up by 4 other mechs shooting at you. - RNG on items is awful, it's really difficult to get anything useful 80% of the time. [b]Multiplayer Experience.[/b] - It's really fun, and enemies are not as oppressive! - Damage is avoidable because you're not being targeted by 5 mechs at once at different time intervals. Although enemy targeting is a bit odd, they do target the first person they see and basically tunnel them until either they die or lose their main target. - Team play really helps with how much loot you can carry out and how fast you can clear the map out, which makes it more likely you can get stuff you actually wanted! - [strike]A major flaw in multiplayer is that 95% of the menus you can use are restricted to one player at a time. If it weren't for that, I'd assume the game was made with multiplayer in mind.[/strike] It is fixed now! - Sharing is caring, you can support allies with stuff you don't use, like ammo, parts, or even a gun you don't like but is Tier 3, so someone might use it! - One person dying ends the game instantly. (Hard+) [b]Non-player amount reliant[/b] - Damage is unavoidable, unless it's 1v1 or endgame, you can't dodge forever, but enemies can shoot forever. As much as I'd love to dodge and respond to all flashy lights indicating I'm about to get shot, it's simply not possible with non-endgame gear. - Endless waves of enemies, and they don't stop coming, and they don't stop coming, and they don't stop coming... - The game forever escalates, even if your mission objective was to clear a map, after it's cleared, you better extract ASAP because even though nothing will attack you or spawn, escalation will grow, powering all enemies up in future missions. - Difficulty levels are terribly made, instead of actual higher danger and more nuances, you just get hit by flat +40% enemy damage and +40% health for enemies. even boss has flat health boost. [h3]Campaign-specific experience (Campaign -> C)[/h3] [b]C1&C2[/b] - Basically same modes, one more simpler and faster and other more complex and a bit longer - C1 30-45 Minute playtime while C2 at most 2 hours - You most likely won't build the mech of your dreams - C1 is easiest while C2 the hardest campaign - Has a very limited pool of mission maps - I NEED AMMO (very little ammo) [b]C3 (New game, same mechs)[/b] - Longest playtime available (2-4 hours) - Base-building mechanics! - You probably will build a mech of your dreams, or at least something that kills really well! - Probably the most balanced campaign because of how much you can play it out! - Has the most distinct pool of mission maps! - You can probably go guns blazing most of the game (plenty of ammo). [h3]Map design and replayability[/h3] Missions are not randomly generated, maps are mostly the same (including enemy placement) on some campaigns more than others. Components and weapons in this game don't really make it feel like I'm playing a much different mech apart from having different-looking swords with a bit different stats or having a gun that is either an AK or an M4, gun is a gun, sword is a sword. That being said, the game does try to salvage this by giving parts random modifiers that do some things like lower weight or buffing stats, but that still lacks, only late-game T4 items give any meaningful attributes, but you won't get more than 1-3 parts a run. [h3]Some other stuff that wouldn't fit elsewhere[/h3] - Campaign+ feels redundant, because unless it's C1, you will probably be done with the game after beating it at that point. - Very limited saves, you can't have two runs on the same campaign at once in either multiplayer or single-player. So make sure you one-shot the campaign if you intend to play with a different squad afterward. - Too much scrolling in the UI + multiplayer menu issues makes it take an extra 5 minutes per between-mission setup. - The game really makes you think about how to efficiently do everything, and it does it very well, like planning out map progressions and such. But you can't really plan the RNG loot factor. - WHY ARE ENEMY MECHS WILLING TO GIVE THEIR LIFE FOR THE CORPORATION?? ARE THEY AI AND NOT PILOTS? EVEN WITHOUT ARMS, THEY WILL FOLLOW YOU UNTIL YOU GIVE THEM SWEET RELEASE OF DEATHH AAAAAAGHH!!!!!11 - [strike]FRIENDLY FIRE: It's annoying, some weapons do it, some don't. it's not Player/Enemy dependant. It's only horrible because it's inconsistent.[/strike] it's now more clear what damages friendlies and what doesn't. [h3]Many things lack explaning![/h3] - [strike]The game won't tell you if your "toggle" guns are on or off unless you can actually see if they're locking on.[/strike] as of recent update, you now have UI confirmation of enabled lock-on weapon. - Some lock-on guns don't actually lock on enemies but turn on shooting, so you might think your torso machine guns will automatically shoot at a locked-on enemy, but they only really shoot at your crosshair, which makes the lock-on thing pointless? - Some map objectives and points of interest are not really clear, like "Allows for more resistance support" Unless you already played the game many times, you will have no idea what going there actually does for you. - Some weapons can be dual-wielded but also be one-hand wielded if your arm is strong enough, but some just straight up don't. (It's not explained, but it's like stats on the hand/weapon are like arm strength/dual-wield strength.) [h3]Final Thoughts[/h3] It's a very good mech-building game, overall very fun with friends! I personally hope to see game development for a long time, because there's lots to improve and make the game much better than ever before! Dev is also very active on their Discord, go take a look! [strike]Since I'm from Poland, I had to basically pay 19 American dollars, or 17.20 euros. It's kind of too much, and with important features like non-lazy difficulty levels, replayability value, and multiplayer QoL lacking, I wouldn't really recommend the game for such a price to my friends[/strike] Price was "Polished" Although if you're really into mech games, you will enjoy your couple of hours with this game!

个人总体评价：游戏目前处于一个 “半成品”状态，核心系统存在严重缺陷，设计与体验严重脱节，其当前质量与售价严重不符。 一、 核心玩法循环崩坏 1. 断裂的经济系统： 第一关获得的信用点在关卡内无处消费，且不继承至后续关卡，导致资源积累无意义。 风险与回报极度失衡：攻击宝箱守卫会永久性增强敌人，但宝箱奖励随机且往往不值一提。 2. 惩罚性的难度曲线： 敌人随战斗变强：玩家战斗越多，敌人变得越强，直接惩罚了“游玩”行为本身，导致玩家不敢探索和战斗。 玩家成长滞后：配件获取困难且升级缓慢，成长速度远跟不上敌人强度的提升，形成“死亡螺旋”。 3. 灾难性的失败惩罚： 死亡后“全副身家”清零（所有配件丢失），而非仅丢失当局资源。这完全否定了玩家的时间投入，带来极强的挫败感，而非“再试一次”的动力。 二、 各系统设计与体验问题 4. 无用的队友与招募系统： 招募的队友无法升级和自定义，性价比极低，在游戏中后期完全沦为累赘。 队友的存在无法改变“玩家被迫单挑一群敌人”的核心困境。 5. 失效且可疑的道具系统： 回复道具无法使用（严重BUG或未完成内容），导致玩家在对局中基本无法进行任何可靠的血量回复，极大地提高了难度和挫败感。 6. 自我矛盾的战前准备： 战前准备有时间限制，与“机甲建造”这一需要深思熟虑的核心乐趣直接冲突，制造了不必要的焦虑，并放大了其他系统的缺陷。 7. 孤芳自赏的联机模式： 在一个玩法基础崩坏、玩家基数极低的冷门游戏中，投入资源开发联机系统是本末倒置。结果自然是 “鬼服”，无人可用，浪费了开发资源。 三、 设计愿景混乱 8. 玩法模式不统一：游戏在第一、二关是“搜打撤”玩法，到第三关却突兀地转变为“经营模拟”，缺乏过渡，让玩家感到困惑和割裂。 9. “缝合怪”式设计：游戏机械地缝合了多种热门机制（Roguelite、机甲建造、联机合作、经营），但未能将这些机制有机地融合成一个协调的整体，导致每个系统都感觉孤立和鸡肋。 总结：游戏唯一的亮点是其工业风的美术风格，但与全面崩坏的核心玩法相比，这仅是杯水车薪。除非进行大刀阔斧的系统级重构，否则这款游戏注定无法摆脱其“冷门”且“令人失望”的标签。 I. Broken Core Gameplay Loop 1. Fractured Economy: Credits earned in the first mission have no use within the level and do not carry over, making resource accumulation meaningless. Severe risk/reward imbalance: Attacking crate guards permanently strengthens enemies, but crate rewards are random and often worthless. 2. Punitive Difficulty Curve: Enemies scale with player combat**: The more you play (fight), the stronger enemies become. This directly punishes the core act of playing, discouraging exploration and combat. Stagnant Player Progression: Parts are hard to find and upgrade slowly. Player power growth falls far behind enemy scaling, creating a "death spiral." 3. Catastrophic Failure Penalty: Death results in a "total wipe"(loss of all collected parts), not just run-specific resources. This completely invalidates the player's time investment, generating extreme frustration instead of the motivation to "try again." II. Flawed System Design & Experience 4. Useless Teammate & Recruitment System: Recruited teammates **cannot be upgraded or customized, offering poor value and becoming a liability by the mid to late game. The system fails to alleviate the core problem of the player being forced to "1v10" enemy groups. 5. Dysfunctional Item System: Healing items cannot be used (a critical bug or unfinished content), leaving players with no reliable means of in-mission health recovery, drastically increasing frustration and artificial difficulty. 6. Self-Defeating Pre-Mission Prep: A time limit on pre-mission preparation directly conflicts with the thoughtful, strategic core joy of "mech building," creating unnecessary stress and exacerbating other system flaws. 7. Pointless Online Multiplayer: Implementing a co-op system in a niche game with a broken core loop and a tiny player base is a misplacement of resources. The inevitable result is a "ghost town" mode that no one uses. III. Lack of Cohesive Vision 8. Inconsistent Gameplay Modes: The game shifts abruptly from a "loot-shoot-extract" gameplay in Missions 1-2 to a "base management sim" in Mission 3, lacking transition and creating a disjointed experience. 9. "Frankenstein" Design: The game mechanically stitches together popular mechanics (Roguelite, mech building, co-op, management) but fails to **organically integrate** them into a cohesive whole. Every system feels isolated and underwhelming. Conclusion: The game's sole redeeming quality is its industrial-punk art style. However, this is a minor merit compared to the comprehensively broken core gameplay. Without a radical, system-level redesign, the game is doomed to remain a "niche" and "disappointing" title.

I had fun with Granvir for a bit, but it has identity issues. Everything about the actual gameplay encourages playing it like Mechwarrior: Slow, hefty machine with a big gun that can alpha strike core enemies in one blast. Everything about the controls and options encourages playing it like Armored Core: Zippy, flying anime mech that dodges enemy attacks. The zippy hypermobility doesn't work, though, because you're never really that mobile, and the mech has a lot of weight and inertia to it(again, kinda like Mechwarrior) and many of the maps(especially the forests) are cluttered with stuff that prevent you from zipping around at-will anyway. It also suffers from the issue that you generally only have two arm slots(I don't think there even are any torsos with more, I certainly never saw any) and about two-thirds of the ranged weapons you find require both those slots. There are also back slot weapons, but you will not get a back slot until you unlock an upgraded torso, and then you have to hope for a good back slot weapon to put there. I think the two-handed weapons existing at all is a mistake without at least having guaranteed back slots on most/all torsos, including the default. Alternately, at least give us some multi-armed torsos so we can experiment more. The game also suffers a bit from some options just being so much better than others(a torso with more slots? Maybe extra cargo space? Why hell yes I will take that over basically anything else you can offer me) that experimentation really isn't very encouraged either. Some stuff also generally feels untuned, like at one point I unlocked regular rebellion air strikes to support me, but they never really did meaningful damage to enemy mechs on the rare occasions they did hit them. Perhaps being able to see health bars or something would help make it more obvious that they're doing something. When you're defending objectives, enemies also drop in literally within spitting distance, which is kinda janky and also means that when those places have emplaced defenses(like the foundries), those defenses never really get to do much. Melee... uhh... it's gonna need to do way more damage to be worth risking getting up close, or ammo has to be way more of a problem. I think Granvir has potential but first it needs to sort out what it wants to be and intensify its efforts to be that.

Granvir stands out as a feature complete indie mech game that feels like a throwback to the older, tactical Armored Core titles of the PS1 and PS2 era. It drops you onto small maps for snappy, intense battles against hordes of AI mechs, balancing high-speed combat with a surprisingly deep strategic management layer. The Good Deep Build Variety: The customization options are robust. You can outfit your mech with everything from standard machine guns, rockets, and shields to specialized lances and even centaur legs. Engaging Strategy Layer: The choices between missions are genuinely tough. You’re constantly balancing time, cash, escalation, and repairs. You’ll frequently have to weigh whether to pay a porter to haul gear, scrap it for fast money, tune up your rig for a brutal fight, or help out locals for reputation points. Fair Roguelike Structure: Unlike a lot of modern roguelikes that force you to fail through multiple cycles just to grind out meta-progression, Granvir respects your time. If you play well, you can reasonably expect to succeed on your very first campaign run. Seamless Co-op: It features quick and easy co-op that makes for a great session with a friend. Just keep in mind that until the final campaign mission, nobody can actually die, so it keeps the stakes friendly while you stick together. Bonus Features: The painting system is incredibly robust, allowing you to tweak individual parts and save your favorite color schemes. The Bad Control Layout Jank: While the controls feel intuitive at first, the scheme leaves a lot to be desired when you change your build. Torso-mounted weapons are a pain to figure out. On more than one occasion, equipping a new weapon system left me entirely unable to fire mid-mission, forcing me to pause for a tedious rebind. Making build adjustments shouldn't feel like a chore. The Verdict Overall, this is an excellent indie gem that cuts out the fluff and delivers on its mechanics. If you're stressed about pulling the trigger, the developer actually offers the first campaign for free under the title Granvir: Zero Front. Honestly, though? Don't bother with the demo just buy the full game. I picked this sucker up on sale for $11, but it is easily worth its full retail asking price of $15. Let’s get real: you’d spend more on an UberEats delivery than you will on this, and you'll get way more hours of enjoyment out of it. Highly recommended.

It's a small indie game about building an incredibly customizable mech, with an equally customizable control scheme that can be as convoluted as you want, or as simple as you can handle. I can't tell you how many times I've face-tanked a bullet after having forgotten about the shield module I've installed for that very purpose, but if I could, it would probably be a big number. As I see it, Granvir's incredible customizability is its main selling point. You've got hover legs, quad legs, sprinter legs, regular legs, legs with rocket boosters, legs with missiles, and even legs with extra storage. And those are just legs. I could talk about torsos, and the many forms and functions they come in, but that's likely longer than I ought to make this review. Point is, there's a lot of mechs you could build in this game, and plenty of synergies to pull together to create your very own off-brand Gundam—or whatever mecha franchise you fancy best. It certainly seems to be inspired in part by so much mecha media, many of which I probably only heard about. Sure, the graphics aren't the best, but that's the cost of an indie budget and a development team that could be probably counted with just one hand (not that I know the exact number, but I know of at least one). The trade-off for these simple graphics is an incredibly active development schedule that launches something new every other week, something which I greatly appreciate. Having an active development team that listens to their community is awesome, and to name a particular example, the recent kick rework turned an otherwise useless mechanic into something actually worth using and is incredibly satisfying to use; and that rework was made possible with the sliding mechanic introduced the update immediately prior! The developers are always adding something new to this game, and while I doubt my voice was the only reason, having something I requested added into the game (the aforementioned kicking rework) is just so incredibly awesome. As an avid mecha game player, I can't recommend Granvir enough. It's not as polished as some other titles, and there are some issues I have with it (like communication in Multiplayer being largely non-functional, besides the pinging mechanic), but they're ultimately minor problems in my eyes. Granvir is a very fun, bite-sized game that has me coming back for more, and at the price I paid it for, it was more than worth it.

In Granvir you're always making tradeoff decisions with the intent of playthroughs being somewhat finite and a bit tense based on your use of time, money, armor, hull, ammo, parts, everything is supposed to factor in. In my experience it's a brilliant concept though often I find myself either finding a build that works and not changing it, which feels like a missed opportunity because of the incredible variety of parts you can put together into some really cool designs. There's a lot of options with campaigns and 'backgrounds' which tweak how your run will go, so probably something I need to look into. For instance, one is a mercenary where you're rewarded for destroying enemies, but start with a debt. This incentivizes an agressive playstyle as the ammo, hull and armor you might lose are compensated by bounties. If you fight well, you'll be pretty much set. ------- Absolutely reccomend this game!

I don't know if I should recommend or not recommend Granvir. It's like Mech Warriors (2,3) but with ammo and currency management - it's a drawback. I really want to love Granvir, but it's just a few steps away from becoming a one-and-done game to a constantly replayable game like ROR. 1. Ammo management doesn't feel fun. I like where the dev was going with the idea of managing your ammo. It costs money to get ammo, so make each bullet count and calculate risk-reward of shooting your gun. The execution is not something I find enjoyable. Most of the time I always end up skipping ammo and rushing for melee weapons without ammo, and saving ammo only for tough battles. It's unclear exactly how much ammo you have, since each gun uses ammo differently so I can't tell how many bullets I have before having to commit to an actual fight. I know it's a technical handwave in order to make it streamline, but right now it's at a point where I cannot figure out when the risks are worth the reward. It just doesn't feel right. I don't even have suggestions on how to fix this. It feels weird. Like I wish I didn't have to worry so much about ammo, or have to worry about it in a different way. I liked the reload timing - it requires careful decision making on whether it's a good idea to reload now or behind a rock. 2. Arena is bad. Initially I liked the idea of the Arena. You fight with parts you unlock throughout the game, and see how far you can go. I feel like it's underdeveloped due to lacking any kind of reward system. Yes, you can get money for winning, but why bother when all the parts are free, and there is nothing you can unlock with the money. Again, another idea that sounds good on paper, but execution is off. I think it would've been cool if I could unlock more parts by winning money in the arena, or have to pay for unlocked parts by winning in the arena. Maybe even have boss rounds where every 5th or 10th round would be an ACE. The other part I also didn't like was the lack of ammo in the arena; ammo complaint again. After a dozen rounds you're out of ammo, and seem stuck. Now I die because of ammo management, not because of lack of skill or proper parts. The loss feels out of my control. Ammo is a dooms day clock ticking down until I run out then die, which again I am FORCED to mitigate with melee weapons. It doesn't feel fun having to be forced. Unfortunately, after looking it through I don't think I can recommend it. It's unfair to compare it to ROR, but I feel like the dev is on to something great. Just a few tweaks and I think it can make the game fantastic.
